name: Singer
baseMeaning: A singer emoji: a figure singing into a microphone with a headset mic.
tldr: Singer 🧑‍🎤: marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: a figure singing into a microphone with a headset mic. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Signing off a voice note with a song 🧑‍🎤

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night.
contextMeanings.example: Claiming the aux cord at a party 🧑‍🎤

contextMeanings.meaning: Used sarcastically it is the gesture with the deadpan delivery: marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, said without believing any of it.

platformNotes.note: In TikTok comments 🧑‍🎤 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🧑‍🎤 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for signing off a voice note with a song, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.

On Discord 🧑‍🎤 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🧑‍🎤 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like claiming the aux cord at a party. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Singer 🧑‍🎤 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like signing off a voice note with a song is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

generationalNotes.note: Older senders use 🧑‍🎤 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 🧑‍🎤 to do the work of signing off a voice note with a song, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night.

Millennials tend to send 🧑‍🎤 deliberately, usually for something like claiming the aux cord at a party, and they read marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🧑‍🎤 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night into it than younger senders are.

warnings.description: The Microphone 🎤 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the microphone stands for the act itself, the singer adds a person doing it. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🧑‍🎤 as something else fairly often: it gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 🧑‍🎤 Singer Emoji Meaning and How to Use It
seoDescription: What 🧑‍🎤 means when people send it, the singer reading, and how to answer it without guessing.

longForm.overview:
What follows is the useful part: the two things the singer is actually for (signing off a voice note with a song and claiming the aux cord at a party), the reading it gets when it is not what the sender meant, and the five tone pages that sit under this one.

There is not a lot to the picture. 🧑‍🎤 is a figure singing into a microphone with a headset mic, added in Unicode 12.1 and filed under person-role. What it does in a message is carry a meaning — here, marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night — without anyone having to write it out.

That plain reading is the one most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, and it lands first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🎤 Microphone: the microphone stands for the act itself, the singer adds a person doing it. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

There are five tone versions of this emoji, and they are not copies of this page. Each one describes the same gesture from inside a different group, because a tone is read as a signal about the sender before the sentence is read.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The common uses are signing off a voice note with a song and claiming the aux cord at a party. The first one is about speed — the picture replaces the explanation, and it lands before the words would have. The second is about tone — the sentence stands on its own, and the emoji is there to change how it reads.

The same emoji in three rooms: a family thread, a work channel, and a dating app. In the first it closes a conversation, in the second it hands something over, in the third it is a joke with an eyebrow raised. The drawing never changes; the expectation of the reader does.

That is also the reason the skin-tone variants are written as their own pages rather than as one page with a table of swatches. A tone is not a setting, and it is read differently.

Look at how often 🧑‍🎤 is used to avoid typing. A question goes out, a question comes back, and in between there is a single picture standing in for an answer that would have taken a sentence. It reads as "marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night", which is fine until it is not.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Watch the picker, and watch the thread. 🧑‍🎤 is easy to send when 🎤 Microphone was meant — the microphone stands for the act itself, the singer adds a person doing it. And the emoji has no business being the whole reply to somebody who has just told you something bad: it reads as "marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night", which is about the gesture rather than about them.

The problem is not the emoji, it is the message underneath it. 🧑‍🎤 gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk, and the drift happens silently. Nobody notices that the meaning changed, because the change was in a picture.

Nor is it a good opener with a stranger. The drawing is cold, and singer gestures have collected a faintly superior edge from being used to reply to other people for years.

Professional settings are the other place to leave it alone. Put 🧑‍🎤 next to somebody's performance, or in a first note to a client, and marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night is the note it reads as — a note that costs more in a workplace than in a group chat.
longForm.howToReply:
Matching works when the message was a reaction: send 🧑‍🎤 back and the tone is confirmed without a word. It does not work when the message was aimed at you. A request, a handover, a nudge — those want a sentence, because two gestures in a row leave the question open.

If you cannot tell how the singer was meant, read the line above it instead. 🧑‍🎤 gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk; the sentence underneath is the part that disambiguates it.

Warmth needs words next to the picture. Something like signing off a voice note with a song sent with 🧑‍🎤 on its own is a coin toss between marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night and something sharper, and the sender never gets to pick which one landed.

faqs.question: What does 🧑‍🎤 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🧑‍🎤 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under singer show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🧑‍🎤 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🧑‍🎤 is used for marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night. The drawing shows a figure singing into a microphone with a headset mic, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🧑‍🎤 and 🎤?
faqs.answer: The microphone stands for the act itself, the singer adds a person doing it. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🧑‍🎤 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, but it gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: signing off a voice note with a song 🧑‍🎤
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: claiming the aux cord at a party 🧑‍🎤
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as marking performance, music taste, or karaoke night, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🧑‍🎤
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets taken for a professional stage performer when it is usually just someone announcing they are going to sing, which is why it shows up as a playful sign-off rather than as music talk more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
